questions.prompt: A warp reads 32 consecutive 4-byte floats starting at byte address 64. How many 32-byte sectors does it touch?
questions.explanation: Bytes 64–191, which is exactly sectors 2, 3, 4 and 5 (aligned).

questions.prompt: Same, but starting at byte address 68. How many sectors?
A warp reads floats with stride 4 (lane l reads element 4l). What is the efficiency, in percent?
questions.explanation: Span 512 bytes, so 16 sectors moved for 128 requested: 25%.

questions.prompt: Why does memory work in fixed-size chunks rather than single words?
options: DRAM activates whole rows and transfers bursts; per-word access would waste most of each burst's overhead
questions.explanation: Row activation and burst transfers make consecutive bytes cheap and isolated bytes expensive.

questions.prompt: All 32 lanes of a warp read the same float. How many sectors does the instruction need?
A memory-bound kernel's loads run at 25% sector efficiency. Roughly how much faster could it get with perfect coalescing?
questions.explanation: It moves 4× the bytes it needs; removing that waste can cut memory time up to 4×.
